Use this scoring rubric: meaning/context/theological distinctions 50 points; completeness and factual/scripture-reference fidelity 30 points; target-language clarity/grammar/idiom 15 points; captions/alt/title/subtitle fidelity 5 points. A score is a review judgment, NOT a measured percentage of accuracy. Accept only a total of at least 95 and no major or critical finding.

A changed doctrinal assertion, negation, attribution, Scripture number, omitted substantive sentence, invented explanation, or untranslated substantive passage is major or critical and must prevent acceptance even when the numerical score is high. Preserve the author's theology rather than correcting it. Quoted Scripture and other quoted substantive prose must be translated into the target language, faithfully conveying the authoritative English as printed. Fidelity means preserving the printed meaning, not retaining English wording. Do not substitute another Bible version or require the translator to copy, retain, or restore English quoted prose as a fidelity workaround. Book names should use conventional target-language forms while exact chapter/verse numbers, ranges and the number and placement of references remain unchanged. An unchanged proper name, established title of a cited work, or identifier is not by itself an untranslated substantive passage; judge its role in context. This exception does not permit leaving quoted prose or translatable article metadata in English. Any substantiated meaning, theology, omission, attribution, or reference error still requires a narrowly scoped correction in the target language. Check paragraph meaning in context, headings, notes, captions, image descriptions, names, figures, and poetry. Do not penalize correct idiomatic expressions for failing to be literal. Do not flag mere stylistic alternatives as errors.

Review only source.html, source.title, source.subtitle, and source.section against the corresponding translation fields. source_context.byline is attribution context only and is rendered separately by the website from the authoritative English metadata. Its absence from the translation is not an omission and must not lower the score or produce a finding. Never request a new byline field or a paragraph such as p.byline. If attribution is already present inside source.html, preserve it in that exact structure. Correction suggestions must preserve source HTML tags, order, nesting, and immutable attributes. Distinguish Scripture references from times of day: an equivalent localized clock rendering, such as 2 pm becoming 14:00 in clear clock context, is not an added or changed Scripture reference.

Return strict JSON with score (integer 0 through 100), passed (boolean), and findings (array). Each finding has severity (minor/major/critical), location, source_quote, translation_quote, and suggested_fix, all textual. Provide concrete evidence for every finding and actionable, narrowly scoped fixes. If there are no substantive problems, return an empty findings array and do not invent criticisms. Do not rewrite the article.

Eight-year-old Jamin wasn’t very smart. Or at least that’s what his older brother told him. Almost daily, brother Kenny found ways to remind Jamin of his shortcomings and laugh at his blunders.

“Jamin, you will never be smart”, Kenny said. Deep inside Jamin felt resigned to a life of muddled trip-ups. Would he always be clumsy? Would he always say things wrong? That’s what Kenny said.

Jamin believed Kenny’s lectures with wide-eyed belief. Kenny was three years older than him, so he must be right. Very well, then Jamin would be simple. Kenny would be smart. Life was not fair. Dad and Mom disliked Kenny’s proud talk and punished him whenever they walked in on one of his speeches. But Kenny had a way of avoiding earshot. So he continued mocking Jamin.

Grandma Otto watched these trials from her rocker on the porch. She was a quiet old lady.

“Jamin, do you know where Kenny is?” Mom asked with a smile. “It’s almost supper time.”

“He went to check his coyote traps. I’ll go find him.”

There was a chill in the air as he tramped up over the lawn, and the sun was growing old as he crossed the border of the woods. The fleeting shadows scurried over the hills. The chill deepened as he stumped further in. He breathed the rich air and followed Kenny’s trail. Eventually, the trail would end up in a meadow, but Jamin hoped he would find Kenny before he had to go that far. The various traps had been checked already, so Jamin knew Kenny had come this way. Jamin trudged on resolutely. His golden head caught the tired beams that fled from the sun as they flickered through the trees. And soon those too had faded leaving behind the musky smell of the woods. The fall webworms had been at work, and their web curtains shuttered from branches overhead.

At length, as the trees subdued and thinned, and the meadow appeared Jamin knew this was the end of his brother’s trap route. If Kenny wasn’t here, he wouldn’t know where else to look.

But Kenny was there. As Jamin clumped into the meadow, he could see a frustrated heap to his right. The heap’s voice had a familiar ring. The heap’s face was lit in pain. The heap was Kenny. “Are you alright? What happened?” Jamin felt strange, seeing Kenny scrunched in the dirt. Kenny was smart. “Did you step in a trap?”

“Yes, Jamin. I..I wasn’t looking where I was going. Help me. Please.”

Jamin bent and found an ankle firmly held in the jaws of a steel trap. Darkness stained the ground around Kenny. Quickly, Jamin’s strong arms pried open the jaws. Kenny reeled free. “Can you walk?”

“Yes. I think so. If you support me, I can hobble along.”

“Dad and Mom will be worried. We’ve missed supper.”

Sure enough, as the brothers hobbled back through the woods, they heard the long calling of their father. Jamin called back, and he was by their side in a moment, seeing the ankle and scooping up Kenny like a hurt sheep. The odd little band hurried home, and the screen door banged shut as Dad swept across the porch. Jamin went to the wash house and scrubbed his hands. He headed for the front door.

“Jamin.” It was Grandma. The porch light showed her in her old rocker. A heavy comforter lay on her shoulders.

“Yes, Grandma?”

“Do you think you are not very smart?”

“That’s what Kenny says.” Jamin squirmed.

“You were strong enough to open the trap, and Kenny wasn’t. You were brave enough to find him in the dark. Lots of young boys wouldn’t be.” Jamin was silent. Grandma Otto rocked some more, then smiled. “God made you the way you are for a reason, Jamin. He made Kenny the way he is for a reason. He has a plan for you, and a place only you can fill, you know.”

Jamin turned and walked into the warm kitchen. He was smiling.

Jamin mwenye umri wa miaka nane hakuwa werevu sana. Au angalau hivyo ndicho alichokisema kaka yake mkubwa. Karibu kila siku, kaka Kenny alitafuta njia za kumkumbusha Jamin mapungufu yake na kucheka makosa yake.

“Jamin, hutawahi kuwa werevu,” alisema Kenny. Ndani kabisa Jamin alihisi kukubali maisha ya makosa ya kuchanganyikiwa. Je, daima atakuwa msongamano? Je, daima atasema maneno vibaya? Hivyo ndicho alichosema Kenny.

Jamin aliamini mafunzo ya Kenny kwa imani yenye macho makubwa. Kenny alikuwa na miaka mitatu zaidi yake, hivyo lazima alikuwa sahihi. Sawa basi, Jamin atakuwa mwepesi wa akili. Kenny atakuwa werevu. Maisha yalikuwa si ya haki. Baba na Mama hawakupendea maneno ya kiburi ya Kenny na wangehubiri kumwadhibu kila walipomkuta akizungumza. Lakini Kenny alikuwa na njia ya kuepuka kusikia. Hivyo aliendelea kumdhihaki Jamin.

Bibi Otto alitazama majaribu haya kutoka kwenye kiti chake cha kuzungusha kwenye korido. Alikuwa mwanamke mzee mwenye unyenyekevu.

“Jamin, unajua Kenny yuko wapi?” Mama aliuliza kwa tabasamu. “Tayari ni karibu wakati wa chakula cha jioni.”

“Alikwenda kukagua mitego yake ya mbweha. Nitaenda kumtafuta.”

Kulikuwa na baridi hewani alipopanda juu juu ya uwanja wa mbuga, na jua lilikuwa likozeeka alipovuka mpaka wa msitu. Vivuli vilivyopita vilikimbilia juu ya milima. Baridi ilizidi wakati alipozama ndani zaidi. Alipumua hewa yenye harufu nzuri na akafuata mfuatano wa Kenny. Mwishowe, mfuatano ungeisha kwenye uwanja wa majani, lakini Jamin alitumaini kumkuta Kenny kabla hajafika huko. Mitego mbalimbali ilishakaguliwa tayari, kwa hivyo Jamin alijua Kenny alikuwa ameipitia njia hii. Jamin alikanyaga kwa msukumo. Kisu chake cha dhahabu kilimwaga mionzi iliyochoka iliyokimbia kutoka jua ilipong'aa katikati ya miti. Na hivi karibuni hata hizo zilikuwa zimepotea zikiweka nyuma harufu ya msitu. Wavumbi wa nyasi walikuwa wameshapeleka kazi yao, na mapazia yao ya wavu yalifungwa kutoka kwa matawi juu.

Hatimaye, wakati miti ilipopunguza nguvu na kuwa nyembamba, na uwanja wa majani ukaonekana, Jamin alijua hii ilikuwa mwisho wa mipango ya mitego ya kaka yake. Ikiwa Kenny hakuwa hapa, hangejua wapi tena kutafuta.

Kwani Kenny alikuwa pale. Alipokuwa Jamin akitoka porini na kuingia kwenye uwanja, aliona gundi iliyochanganyikiwa kulia kwake. Sauti ya gundi hiyo ilikuwa ya kumfahamisha. Uso wa gundi ulikuwa umeangaziwa kwa maumivu. Gundi hilo lilikuwa Kenny. “Uko sawa? Nini kilitokea?” Jamin alihisi kushangaza, akimuona Kenny ameegeshwa katika udongo. Kenny alikuwa werevu. “Ulishika mtego?”

“Ndiyo, Jamin. Mimi… sikuuangalia nilipotembea. Nisaidie. Tafadhali.”

Jamin alikunjua na kupata kiwiko kikishikiliwa kwa nguvu mdomoni mwa mtego wa chuma. Giza lilikuwa limechafua ardhi karibu na Kenny. Mara moja, mikono imara ya Jamin ilifungua kwa nguvu mdomo wa mtego. Kenny aliondoka kwa haraka. “Unaweza kutembea?”

“Ndio. Nahisi hivyo. Ukinitulia, nitaweza kutapika polepole.”

“Baba na Mama watakuwa na wasiwasi. Tumechelewa chakula cha jioni.”

Kama ilivyotarajiwa, wakati ndugu hao walipokuwa wakitapika kwa kurudi porini, walisikia sauti ndefu ya kuwaita ya baba yao. Jamin alijibu, na alimtokea upande wao kwa sekunde, akiangalia kiwiko na kumchukua Kenny kama kondoo aliyejeruhiwa. Kikundi hicho kidogo kilikimbia nyumbani, na mlango wa skrini ukagongana wakati Baba alipitia korido. Jamin alikwenda chumbini kuoshea mikono yake. Alielekea kwenye mlango wa mbele.

“Jamin.” Alikuwa Bibi. Taa ya korido ilimuonyesha akiwa kwenye kiti chake cha kuzungusha. Jasi nzito lilikuwa juu ya mabega yake.

“Ndio, Bibi?”

“Je, unadhani hauwezi kuwa werevu?”

“Hivyo ndicho Kenny anavyosema.” Jamin alizunguka kwa aibu.

“Ulikuwa na nguvu kabisa kufungua mtego, na Kenny hakufanya hivyo. Ulikuwa na ujasiri wa kumtafuta gizani. Wanazuri wengi wasingekuwa na hayo.” Jamin aliketi kimya. Bibi Otto alizungusha kiti kidogo zaidi, kisha akatabasamu. “Mungu alikuumba jinsi ulivyo kwa sababu fulani, Jamin. Alimuumba Kenny jinsi alivyo kwa sababu fulani. Ana mpango kwa ajili yako, na nafasi ambayo ni yako pekee tu inayoweza kuijaza, unajua.”

Jamin aligeuka na kuingia jikoni lenye joto. Alikuwa akitabasamu.

How unbelievable it is that God can take a wretched sinner, void of the fear of the Lord, and turn him into a blood-washed saint and preacher of the gospel! In this story, we see God’s life-changing power at work in our hymn writer’s life.

In the small cemetery of a churchyard in Olney, England, stands a granite tombstone with this inscription, written by Newton himself before his death:

John Newton, once an infidel and libertine, a servant of slaves in Africa, was, by the rich mercy of our Lord and Savior Jesus Christ, preserved, restored, pardoned, and appointed to preach the faith he had long labored to destroy!

This epitaph aptly describes the unusual and colorful life of this man, one of the great evangelical preachers of the eighteenth century. His testimony was, “By the grace of God, I am what I am!”

“Amazing Grace” was a hymn published in 1779, with words written in 1772 by the English poet and Anglican clergyman John Newton (1725–1807). “Amazing Grace” is probably the most beloved hymn of the last two centuries. This hymn is estimated to be performed 10 million times annually. It has appeared on over 11,000 albums and translated into about 60 languages. It was referenced in Harriet Beecher Stowe’s anti-slavery novel Uncle Tom’s Cabin. It had a surge in popularity during two of America’s greatest crises: the Civil War and the Vietnam War.

Ironically, this stirring song, closely associated with the African-American community, was written by a former slave trader, John Newton.

John was born on July 24, 1725, in Wapping, England, to a seafaring father, John Newton, Sr., and a devout Christian mother, Elizabeth Newton. His father loved him but was gone at sea most of the time. On the other hand, his mother was tender and nurturing, teaching him the Word of God. She would instruct him in memorizing the Bible whole chapters at a time and took him to church. Unfortunately, when he was almost seven, his mother died of tuberculosis. His father remarried a short time later and sent him to a boarding school. During his time at the boarding school, he made bad friends. His character disintegrated to the point that he was dismissed from one school and moved to another. By the time he was 11 years old, the boarding schools didn’t want him, so his father took him along to sea. He spent the next six years on the Atlantic Ocean with his father.

When John was 17, his father arranged to send him to Jamaica for a well-paying job overseeing a plantation. On his way, while waiting for the ship’s departure, John received an invitation to the home of some old-time friends, the Catletts. It was in this home that John’s mother had died ten years earlier. As he reacquainted himself with them, he got to know their daughter, Mary. John and Mary’s mothers were best of friends. John had been invited to stay four days, but he stayed two weeks and missed the ship to Jamaica.

At age 18, John was conscripted into the Royal Navy, and his life went from bad to worse. He wanted to return and see Mary, so he deserted the ship but was caught, publicly flogged, and laid in irons. His life on the ship was so profane that even the other ungodly sailors cringed at his curses and blasphemies. He gained the title “The Great Blasphemer” and was such an unwanted man on the ship that he was sent to work on a slave ship.

One of the owners of the slave ship where he now worked, offered John a job once they reached the African coast. However, once on shore, he was tied up and forced to work with little food, clothing, or shelter. He sent several letters back to his father during this time, pleading for help.

A ship called The Greyhound was sailing near the coast, which John had now called home. The captain had been instructed by John’s father to look for his son. The ship, while being almost too far from shore to trade, decided to give trading a try. A friend of John’s rowed out from shore to trade. As he turned to leave, the captain asked him whether he knew anyone named John Newton. He did to the captain’s surprise, and John was brought on board to go home.

On board the ship, Newton picked up a copy of Thomas á Kempis’s Christian classic, The Imitation of Christ. He had never encountered anything like it, and he began to wonder if the Christian claims might be true. That night, on March 10, 1748, a fierce storm nearly swamped the ship. Men, animals, and provisions were swept overboard. The storm awakened Newton, the ship’s rotten timbers broken by the waves and floodwater swirling into his cabin. John prayed for the first time in years.

The Greyhound thrashed about in the North Atlantic storm for over 11 days. With little hope of survival, the sailors mechanically worked the pumps, trying to keep the vessel afloat. On the eleventh day of the storm, John was too exhausted to pump, so he was tied to the helm, where he did his best to hold the ship to its course. From one o’clock until midnight, he was at the helm. He feared he was going to die, and if the Christian faith were true, then he surely would not be forgiven. He reflected on all he had done over the past few years. His life seemed as ruined and wrecked as the battered ship he was trying to steer through the storm. During those long and grueling hours, Newton cried out to God like he never had before, and that was the turning point in his life.

That was a day John Newton remembered ever after. “On that day, the Lord sent from on high and delivered me out of deep waters.” Over 50 years later, John wrote in his diary on March 21, 1805: “Not well able to write; but I endeavor to observe the return of this day with humiliation, prayer, and praise.”

Only God’s amazing grace could take a rude, profane, slave-trading sailor and transform him into a child of God. John never ceased to stand in awe of God’s work in his life. He took an interest in prayer, reading and meditating on the Scriptures, and only speaking words pleasing to God.

On his return home, Mary and her parents recognized the change the Lord had brought in John. The two were married on February 1, 1750.

For the next four years, Newton was captain of his own slave ship. This occupation kept him separated from Mary for months at a time. While they were apart, the two corresponded constantly. In his letters, John repeatedly wrote how their love and marriage increased his thankfulness and gratefulness to the Lord. “... When I indulge myself with a particular thought of you, it usually carries me on farther and brings me upon my knees to bless the Lord for giving me such a treasure and to pray for your peace and welfare”

John endeavored to “Christianize” his slave ship by holding Sunday services for his crew of 30 sin-hardened men. He made three more voyages to bring slaves from Africa to North America. As he planned his fourth trip, he became sick with malaria. God used this sickness to end his involvement in the slave trade.

As John began a new chapter in his life, he felt called to be a minister. For more than 50 years, he preached the gospel and was one of the most influential men of his day.

John Newton often composed a hymn to go with his Sunday evening services. In 1779, 280 of these were collected and combined with 68 hymns by Newton’s friend and parishioner, William Cowper, and published as the Olney Hymns. The most famous of all the Olney Hymns, “Faith’s Review and Expectation”, grew out of David’s exclamation in 1 Chronicles 17:16-17. We know it today as “Amazing Grace”. “Amazing Grace” originally had six stanzas, and the last verse was added about a century later. Most hymnals have four or five of these verses.

As minister in the church, John continued to be more and more troubled by the slave trade that was still going on. In 1788, 34 years after he left the slave trade, He wrote a book entitled Thoughts Upon the African Slave Trade and sent it to all the members of parliament. This book brought an awareness to the public of the evils of the slave trade. He quotes this, “Needless to say, the capturing, selling and transporting of black slaves to the plantations in the West Indies and America was a cruel and vicious way of life.” With the help and providence of God, John saw the day, several months before his death, in 1807, when slavery was officially banned from England.

When John was in his sixties, his beloved wife Mary passed away. This was a great trial for John, and he spent the remaining 17 years of his life without her.

After John suffered a stroke and shortly before his death, a spokesman for the church encouraged Newton to consider retiring from preaching because of failing health, eyesight, and memory. John replied, “What, shall the old African blasphemer stop while he can still speak? I will continue to preach. Although my memory’s fading, I remember two things very clearly: I am a great sinner, and Christ is a great Savior.”

The last words of John Newton as he lay on his deathbed were as follows: “I am still in the land of the dying; I shall be in the land of the living soon.”

The tune “Amazing Grace” is an early American folk melody. It was first known as a plantation melody entitled “Loving Lambs”. This tune was first published in 1831 in the book The Virginia Harmony. The majority of hymn books published after this time included this song. In 1910, Edwin O. Excell added the last verse, which eventually replaced the last three original verses of the song. His edition of the song is most common in our hymnals today. Several other Olney hymns by Newton continue to be sung today, including “How Sweet the Name of Jesus Sounds” and “Glorious Things of Thee are Spoken”.

Πόσο απίστευτο είναι ότι ο Θεός μπορεί να πάρει έναν αξιοθρήνητο αμαρτωλό, χωρίς φόβο Κυρίου, και να τον μετατρέψει σε έναν σαρκικά λουσμένο άγιο και κήρυκα του ευαγγελίου! Σε αυτή την ιστορία βλέπουμε τη ζωοποιό δύναμη του Θεού να ενεργεί στη ζωή του δημιουργού του ύμνου μας.

Στο μικρό νεκροταφείο μιας εκκλησίας στο Olney της Αγγλίας, στέκεται ένας γρανιτένιος τάφος με αυτήν την επιγραφή, γραμμένη από τον ίδιο τον Newton πριν από τον θάνατό του:

John Newton, κάποτε άθεος και άσωτος, υπηρέτης σκλάβων στην Αφρική, διατηρήθηκε, αποκαταστάθηκε, συγχωρήθηκε και ορίστηκε, με το πλούσιο έλεος του Κυρίου και Σωτήρα μας Ιησού Χριστού, να κηρύξει τη πίστη που εδώ και καιρό προσπάθησε να καταστρέψει!

Αυτό το επίγραμμα περιγράφει εύστοχα την ασυνήθιστη και πολύχρωμη ζωή αυτού του ανθρώπου, ενός από τους μεγάλους ευαγγελικούς κήρυκες του δέκατου όγδοου αιώνα. Η μαρτυρία του ήταν: «Χάρη στο Θεό, είμαι αυτό που είμαι!»

Το «Amazing Grace» ήταν ένας ύμνος που δημοσιεύθηκε το 1779, με λόγια γραμμένα το 1772 από τον Άγγλο ποιητή και αγγλικανό κληρικό John Newton (1725–1807). Το «Amazing Grace» είναι πιθανότατα ο πιο αγαπημένος ύμνος των τελευταίων δύο αιώνων. Υπολογίζεται ότι αυτός ο ύμνος εκτελείται 10 εκατομμύρια φορές ετησίως. Έχει εμφανιστεί σε πάνω από 11.000 άλμπουμ και έχει μεταφραστεί σε περίπου 60 γλώσσες. Αναφέρεται στο αντιδουλεμπορικό μυθιστόρημα της Harriet Beecher Stowe, Uncle Tom’s Cabin. Είχε έξαρση δημοφιλίας κατά τη διάρκεια δύο από τις μεγαλύτερες κρίσεις της Αμερικής: του Εμφυλίου Πολέμου και του Πολέμου του Βιετνάμ.

Είναι ειρωνικό ότι αυτό το συγκινητικό τραγούδι, στενά συνδεδεμένο με την αφροαμερικανική κοινότητα, γράφτηκε από έναν πρώην δουλεμπόρο, τον John Newton.

Ο John γεννήθηκε στις 24 Ιουλίου 1725 στο Wapping της Αγγλίας, από ναυτικό πατέρα, John Newton, Sr., και μια ευσεβή μητέρα, την Elizabeth Newton. Ο πατέρας τον αγαπούσε αλλά απουσίαζε στη θάλασσα το μεγαλύτερο μέρος του χρόνου. Αντίθετα, η μητέρα του ήταν στοργική και τρυφερή, διδάσκοντάς τον τον Λόγο του Θεού. Τον δίδασκε να αποστηθίζει ολόκληρα κεφάλαια της Βίβλου και τον πήγαινε στην εκκλησία. Δυστυχώς, όταν ήταν σχεδόν επτά ετών, η μητέρα του πέθανε από φυματίωση. Ο πατέρας ξαναπαντρεύτηκε λίγο αργότερα και τον έστειλε σε οικοτροφείο. Κατά τη διάρκεια του χρόνου του στο οικοτροφείο, έκανε κακές παρέες. Ο χαρακτήρας του διαλύθηκε σε τέτοιο βαθμό που αποβλήθηκε από ένα σχολείο και μεταφέρθηκε σε άλλο. Όταν ήταν 11 ετών, τα οικοτροφεία δεν τον ήθελαν πλέον, οπότε ο πατέρας τον πήρε μαζί του στη θάλασσα. Πέρασε τα επόμενα έξι χρόνια στον Ατλαντικό με τον πατέρα του.

Όταν ο John ήταν 17, ο πατέρας του διοργάνωσε να τον στείλει στη Τζαμάικα για μια καλά αμειβόμενη θέση εποπτείας μιας φυτείας. Καθ’ οδόν, ενώ περίμενε την αναχώρηση του πλοίου, ο John προσκλήθηκε στο σπίτι κάποιων παλιών φίλων, των Catlett. Ήταν σε αυτό το σπίτι όπου η μητέρα του είχε πεθάνει δέκα χρόνια νωρίτερα. Καθώς ξανασυνδέθηκε μαζί τους, ήρθε σε επαφή με την κόρη τους, τη Mary. Οι μητέρες του John και της Mary ήταν οι καλύτερες φίλες. Ο John είχε προσκληθεί να μείνει τέσσερις ημέρες, αλλά έμεινε δύο εβδομάδες και έχασε το πλοίο για τη Τζαμάικα.

Σε ηλικία 18 ετών, ο John επιστρατεύτηκε στο Βασιλικό Ναυτικό και η ζωή του χειροτέρεψε. Ήθελε να επιστρέψει και να δει τη Mary, οπότε φυγοστράφησε από το πλοίο αλλά τον συνέλαβαν, τον μαστίγωσαν δημοσίως και τον έδεσαν με αλυσίδες. Η ζωή του στο πλοίο ήταν τόσο βέβηλη που ακόμη και οι υπόλοιποι άθρησκοι ναύτες σφίγγανε τα δόντια μπροστά στις κατάρες και τις βλασφημίες του. Έλαβε τον τίτλο «Ο Μεγάλος Βλασφημητής» και ήταν τόσο ανεπιθύμητος στο πλοίο που τον έστειλαν να εργάζεται σε δουλεμπορικό πλοίο.

Ένας από τους ιδιοκτήτες του δουλεμπορικού πλοίου όπου τώρα δούλευε, του πρόσφερε εργασία όταν έφταναν στην αφρικανική ακτή. Ωστόσο, μόλις βγήκε στην ξηρά, τον έδεσαν και τον ανάγκασαν να εργάζεται με ελάχιστο φαγητό, ρούχα ή καταφύγιο. Έστειλε αρκετές επιστολές στον πατέρα του εκείνη την περίοδο, ικετεύοντας για βοήθεια.

Ένα πλοίο με το όνομα The Greyhound έπλεε κοντά στην ακτή που ο John είχε πλέον αποκαλέσει σπίτι. Ο καπετάνιος είχε λάβει εντολή από τον πατέρα του John να ψάξει για τον γιο του. Το πλοίο, αν και σχεδόν πολύ μακριά από την ακτή για εμπόριο, αποφάσισε να επιχειρήσει την ανταλλαγή. Ένας φίλος του John πήγε με βάρκα από την ακτή για εμπόριο. Καθώς γύριζε να φύγει, ο καπετάνιος τον ρώτησε αν γνώριζε κάποιον που να ονομάζεται John Newton. Εκείνος απάντησε, προς έκπληξη του καπετάνιου, ότι ναι, και ο John επιβιβάστηκε για να επιστρέψει σπίτι.

Επάνω στο πλοίο, ο Newton άρπαξε ένα αντίτυπο του χριστιανικού κλασικού του Thomas á Kempis, The Imitation of Christ. Δεν είχε συναντήσει ποτέ κάτι τέτοιο και άρχισε να αναρωτιέται αν οι χριστιανικές αξιώσεις ίσως ήταν αληθινές. Εκείνη τη νύχτα, στις 10 Μαρτίου 1748, μια σφοδρή καταιγίδα σχεδόν αναποδογύρισε το πλοίο. Άνδρες, ζώα και προμήθειες σάρωσαν στη θάλασσα. Η καταιγίδα ξύπνησε τον Newton, τα σαθρά δοκάρια του πλοίου σπασμένα από τα κύματα και τα ορμητικά νερά να περιστρέφονται στην καμπίνα του. Ο John προσευχήθηκε για πρώτη φορά εδώ και χρόνια.

The Greyhound αναταράχθηκε στη Βόρεια Ατλαντική καταιγίδα για πάνω από 11 μέρες. Με λίγες ελπίδες επιβίωσης, οι ναύτες χειρίζονταν μηχανικά τις αντλίες, προσπαθώντας να κρατήσουν το σκάφος στην επιφάνεια. Την ενδέκατη μέρα της καταιγίδας, ο John ήταν πολύ εξαντλημένος για να αντλεί, οπότε τον έδεσαν στο τιμόνι, όπου έκανε ό,τι καλύτερο μπορούσε για να κρατήσει το πλοίο στην πορεία του. Από τη μία μέχρι τα μεσάνυχτα, ήταν στο τιμόνι. Φοβόταν ότι θα πέθαινε, και αν η χριστιανική πίστη ήταν αληθινή, τότε σίγουρα δεν θα του συγχωρούνταν. Σκέφτηκε όλα όσα είχε κάνει τα τελευταία χρόνια. Η ζωή του φαινόταν τόσο κατεστραμμένη και συντριμμένη όσο το χτυπημένο πλοίο που προσπαθούσε να οδηγήσει μέσα στην καταιγίδα. Κατά τις μακριές και βασανιστικές αυτές ώρες, ο Newton αναφώνησε προς τον Θεό όπως ποτέ πριν, και αυτό ήταν το σημείο καμπής στη ζωή του.

Αυτή ήταν μια μέρα που ο John Newton θυμόταν για πάντα. «Εκείνη την ημέρα, ο Κύριος έστειλε από ψηλά και με έβγαλε από βαθιά ύδατα.» Πάνω από 50 χρόνια αργότερα, ο John έγραψε στο ημερολόγιό του στις 21 Μαρτίου 1805: «Δεν είμαι σε θέση να γράψω καλά· αλλά προσπαθώ να τηρήσω την επανεμφάνιση αυτής της ημέρας με ταπείνωση, προσευχή και δοξολογία.»

Μόνο η θαυμαστή χάρη του Θεού μπορούσε να πάρει έναν αγροίκο, βέβηλο δουλεμπόρο ναύτη και να τον μεταμορφώσει σε παιδί του Θεού. Ο John δεν έπαψε ποτέ να στέκεται έκθαμβος για το έργο του Θεού στη ζωή του. Έδειξε ενδιαφέρον για την προσευχή, την ανάγνωση και τον στοχασμό στις Γραφές και να λέει μόνο λόγια ευάρεστα στον Θεό.

Κατά την επιστροφή του στο σπίτι, η Mary και οι γονείς της αναγνώρισαν την αλλαγή που ο Κύριος είχε φέρει στον John. Οι δύο παντρεύτηκαν την 1η Φεβρουαρίου 1750.

Για τα επόμενα τέσσερα χρόνια, ο Newton ήταν καπετάνιος του δικού του δουλεμπορικού πλοίου. Αυτή η απασχόληση τον χώριζε από τη Mary για μήνες κάθε φορά. Όταν ήταν χώρια, οι δύο αντάλλασσαν συνεχώς επιστολές. Στις επιστολές του, ο John έγραφε επανειλημμένα πόσο η αγάπη και ο γάμος τους αύξαγαν την ευγνωμοσύνη του προς τον Κύριο. «... Όταν επιτρέπω στον εαυτό μου μια συγκεκριμένη σκέψη για σένα, συνήθως με μεταφέρει παραπέρα και με φέρνει στα γόνατα να ευλογήσω τον Κύριο για το ότι μου έδωσε έναν τέτοιο θησαυρό και να προσευχηθώ για την ειρήνη και την ευημερία σου.»

Ο John επιχείρησε να «χριστιανοποιήσει» το δουλεμπορικό του διοργανώνοντας κυριακάτικες λατρείες για το πλήρωμά του από 30 σκληραγωγημένους άνδρες. Πραγματοποίησε ακόμη τρία ταξίδια για να μεταφέρει σκλάβους από την Αφρική στη Βόρεια Αμερική. Καθώς σχεδίαζε το τέταρτο ταξίδι του, αρρώστησε από ελονοσία. Ο Θεός χρησιμοποίησε αυτή την ασθένεια για να τερματίσει την εμπλοκή του στο δουλεμπόριο.

Καθώς ο John ξεκινούσε ένα νέο κεφάλαιο στη ζωή του, ένιωθε κλήση να γίνει κληρικός. Για πάνω από 50 χρόνια κήρυττε το ευαγγέλιο και ήταν ένας από τους πιο επιδραστικούς άνδρες της εποχής του.

Ο John Newton συχνά συνέθετε έναν ύμνο για τις κυριακάτικες εσπερινές λατρείες του. Το 1779, 280 από αυτούς συλλέχθηκαν και συνδυάστηκαν με 68 ύμνους από τον φίλο και ενορίτη του Newton, William Cowper, και δημοσιεύθηκαν ως οι Olney Hymns. Ο πιο διάσημος από όλους τους Olney Hymns, «Faith’s Review and Expectation», προέκυψε από την εξομολόγηση του Δαβίδ σε 1 Παραλειπομένων 17:16-17. Τον γνωρίζουμε σήμερα ως «Amazing Grace». Το «Amazing Grace» αρχικά είχε έξι στροφές, και ο τελευταίος στίχος προστέθηκε περίπου έναν αιώνα αργότερα. Τα περισσότερα υμνολόγια διαθέτουν τέσσερις ή πέντε από αυτές τις στροφές.

Ως ιερέας της εκκλησίας, ο John ανησυχούσε όλο και περισσότερο για το δουλεμπόριο που εξακολουθούσε να υφίσταται. Το 1788, 34 χρόνια αφότου έφυγε από το δουλεμπόριο, έγραψε ένα βιβλίο με τίτλο Thoughts Upon the African Slave Trade και το έστειλε σε όλα τα μέλη του Κοινοβουλίου. Αυτό το βιβλίο έφερε στη δημόσια σφαίρα την επίγνωση για τα κακά του δουλεμπορίου. Έγραψε: «Δεν χρειάζεται να πούμε ότι η σύλληψη, η πώληση και η μεταφορά μαύρων σκλάβων στις φυτείες στις Δυτικές Ινδίες και την Αμερική ήταν ένας σκληρός και διεφθαρμένος τρόπος ζωής.» Με τη βοήθεια και τη πρόνοια του Θεού, ο John είδε την ημέρα, μερικούς μήνες πριν από το θάνατό του, το 1807, όταν η δουλεία απαγορεύθηκε επίσημα στην Αγγλία.

Όταν ο John ήταν στα εξήντα, η πολυαγαπημένη του σύζυγος Mary απεβίωσε. Αυτό ήταν μεγάλο δοκίμιο για τον John, και πέρασε τα υπόλοιπα 17 χρόνια της ζωής του χωρίς εκείνη.

Μετά από ένα εγκεφαλικό επεισόδιο και λίγο πριν από τον θάνατό του, ένας εκπρόσωπος της εκκλησίας παρότρυνε τον Newton να σκεφτεί να αποσυρθεί από το κήρυγμα λόγω επιδεινούμενης υγείας, όρασης και μνήμης. Ο John απάντησε: «Τι, θα σταματήσει ο παλιός Αφρικανός βλασφημητής ενώ ακόμη μπορεί να μιλήσει; Θα συνεχίσω να κηρύττω. Παρότι η μνήμη μου σβήνει, θυμάμαι δύο πράγματα πολύ καθαρά: Είμαι μεγάλος αμαρτωλός, και ο Χριστός είναι μεγάλος Σωτήρας.»

Τα τελευταία λόγια του John Newton καθώς βρισκόταν στο προσκεφάλι του ήταν τα εξής: «Είμαι ακόμη στη χώρα των πεθαμένων· σύντομα θα είμαι στη χώρα των ζώντων.»

Η μελωδία του «Amazing Grace» είναι μια πρώιμη αμερικανική λαϊκή μελωδία. Ήταν αρχικά γνωστή ως φυτείας μελωδία με τον τίτλο «Loving Lambs». Αυτή η μελωδία δημοσιεύθηκε για πρώτη φορά το 1831 στο βιβλίο The Virginia Harmony. Η πλειονότητα των υμνολογίων που δημοσιεύθηκαν μετά από αυτή την περίοδο περιλάμβαναν αυτό το τραγούδι. Το 1910, ο Edwin O. Excell πρόσθεσε τον τελευταίο στίχο, ο οποίος τελικά αντικατέστησε τους τρεις τελευταίους αρχικούς στίχους του τραγουδιού. Η έκδοσή του του τραγουδιού είναι η πιο συνηθισμένη στα υμνολόγιά μας σήμερα. Διάφοροι άλλοι Olney Hymns του Newton εξακολουθούν να ψάλλονται σήμερα, συμπεριλαμβανομένων των «How Sweet the Name of Jesus Sounds» και «Glorious Things of Thee are Spoken».

“Dr. Waldron, Elsie needs help!” Elsie’s husband was adamant, almost angry, as he stared at me. On the other hand, Elsie stared at the floor, almost as though she wasn’t present. I had never met either of the couple before and was struggling just a little to figure out what was needed from me to help her.

“What is going on?” I asked as I flipped through her chart. This was still in the days of paper charts, and I headed to the lab section of her chart. There wasn’t anything too crazy that I could see there—her liver enzymes were a little elevated, but otherwise, everything seemed OK.

“It’s her drinking!” Her husband told me. “She is drinking more and more every night. She won’t go out except to get whiskey. She drinks till she passes out every night and has to have something every morning to get her started.”

“Is that true?” I asked Elsie, feeling like a judge overseeing a jury trial.

“Yes,” she said. Her face was emotionless, and I couldn’t tell if she wanted to be there or not.

“Do you want help?” I asked her. This was a loaded question. Many people who struggle with alcoholism aren’t ready to break free from its vice-like hold on them. Maybe Elsie was different.

“I guess so,” she said, indifferently. Once again, I couldn’t tell whether she wanted to be there or not.

“At the rate at which you are drinking, you will kill yourself within a year – maybe two at best – if you don’t give up alcohol entirely,” I told her. “If you want to, I will try to find you an inpatient program to detox you and get you off of alcohol.”

“She’s ready,” he husband said firmly.

When dealing with someone who drinks heavily, it is crucial that they don’t simply stop drinking without medical support. Abrupt cessation of alcohol use causes the body to go into withdrawal which can produce a state called Delirium Tremens and even seizures.

I stepped out of the exam room and to make phone calls. It is never easy to find a place for someone to attempt to rehabilitate from any kind of substances, and it was over an hour and a half before I found a facility that was willing to take Elsie and try to help her get off of the whiskey.

I sighed as I reentered her exam room. I had been afraid that I wouldn’t find anywhere for her to go.

I told them about the plan, and her husband nodded vigorously, while Elise continued to stare silently at the floor. “Can we pray together before you go?” I asked them, and when they nodded assent, I prayed with them, asking for freedom and Jesus’ presence in both of their lives.

They left my office with marching orders and directions on where to go. I had a happy glow about me for the rest of the morning, knowing that I had gone the extra mile and had really made a difference in this middle-aged couple’s life.

Around 2 pm, I got a call from the rehab facility. They hadn’t seen even a shadow of Elsie or her husband, which was surprising, since it was a bright sunny day and the facility wasn’t that far away. With a sinking feeling, I dialed the couple’s phone number.

“She won’t go!” Her husband told me. “She tells me that she told me this ahead of time. She’ll try to cut back, but she isn’t willing to go into a rehab facility or any such thing. I guess just tell them that we’ll let them know if she changes her mind.”

My nurse called the rehab facility and told them the bad news, and I sat down in my chair, stunned. What else could I have done? Was there a solution for Elsie—something different that I could have said that would have made a difference in her life?

About a year later, I received the sad news that Elsie had died at home. I was certain that things would have been different if she had gone to rehab and if she had given control to Jesus. None of that had happened, and I felt cynicism pushing into my heart.

Cynicism

We live in an age of cynicism. In ancient Greece, the cynics were an odd assortment of men who specialized in being grouchy and saying mean (they would have said truthful) things to people. They often dressed in rags and behaved in such a way that most of the polite Athenians did not want to be close to them.

Today, cynicism means a tendency to believe the worst about people and circumstances. Cynical people believe that all people are motivated purely by selfishness and that bad events will tend to prevail.

Many young doctors are idealistic and very hopeful. They believe that if they exert the utmost effort, they can make a real, positive impact on their patient’s lives. Unfortunately, as time goes by and they try their hardest and their patients don’t change, they can give up. These doctors still try, but they no longer really hope that their efforts will make much of a difference.

It seems as though people who get involved with politics often have the best of intentions. They see this as a path to changing society for the better. Unfortunately, as time goes by and the faces in charge change, the policies don’t really change, they tend to become cynical.

Sometimes this cynicism is directed against all politicians. Sometimes it is only anger directed against members of the party that opposes their party’s positions. Hope is replaced by cynicism.

Cynicism in the Bible

If there is a book in the Bible that seems to have been written by a cynical man, it is the book of Ecclesiastes. The Preacher, who we understand to be Solomon, lists all of the things that he endeavored in an attempt to find joy.

In chapter 2:17-23 Solomon describes work as futile. He finishes by saying, “For what hath man of all his labour, and of the vexation of his heart, wherein he hath laboured under the sun? For all his days are sorrows, and his travail grief; yea, his heart taketh not rest in the night. This is also vanity.” (Ecclesiastes 2:22,23)

He saw the world as being dominated by tyrants and there was little that the people could do about it. Solomon went so far as to say that political power was meaningless “Better is a poor and a wise child than an old and foolish king, who will no more be admonished. For out of prison he cometh to reign; whereas also he that is born in his kingdom becometh poor” (Ecclesiastes 4:13).

In Ecclesiastes 6:6, he seems to disparage long life. “Yea, though he live a thousand years twice told, yet hath he seen no good: do not all go to one place?”

Of course, he finishes his short book with the instruction to remember our Creator in the days of our youth. There is a blessing for those who choose to focus on God when they have a little bit of energy left and not, when they are old and jaded, like Solomon.

Later on, it almost seemed as though God had given up on His people. He still sent prophets to them, but He knew without a doubt that the people would refuse to respond. “Therefore thou shalt speak all these words unto them; but they will not hearken to thee: thou shalt also call unto them; but they will not answer thee” (Jeremiah 7:27).

Even in the New Testament, Paul told Timothy that the time was coming when people would no longer listen to sound doctrine. “For the time will come when they will not endure sound doctrine; but after their own lusts shall they heap to themselves teachers, having itching ears;” (2 Timothy 4:3).

By picking and choosing these passages, we can come away with a very gloomy view of the future and, more specifically, of human’s willingness to change. It seems there is little point of investing ourselves in the people around us. They are full of woe and are as likely to change as a chipmunk is to master differential calculus.

The Opposite of Cynicism

The opposite of cynicism is hope. It is the belief that the future could be better.

It is interesting that the Apostle Paul spoke of tribulations in the Epistle to the Romans, “And not only so, but we glory in tribulations also: knowing that tribulation worketh patience; and patience, experience; and experience, hope: and hope maketh not ashamed; because the love of God is shed abroad in our hearts by the Holy Ghost which is given unto us” (Romans 5:3-5).

We may not have reached the place where we glory in the trials we experience, but certainly, they should bring us these other things that he mentions. For, we grow in patience and experience, even as we deal with trials, but more than that, we come to realize that we have hope for tomorrow because we serve a great God.

The contrast in the story of the Prodigal Son in Luke 15 teaches us much about hope. The father and the older brother were strikingly different in their attitudes.

The father had never given up hope – he knew that his son had failed him and gone far from what he knew was right and yet, the father still desired to see the prodigal come to himself and return home.

On the other hand, the older brother not only had no hope for his younger brother, but he was also angry with him. The prodigal had wasted his money, he had lived in sin, and now, he had returned home just because he was out of money.

Certainly, there was no reason to trust the younger son. Yet, that is exactly what our Heavenly Father does for us.

Look for Hope in the Right Places

Part of the problem is that we look for hope in the wrong places. A number of years ago, a presidential candidate ran for office under the slogan “Hope and Change,” and yet, even though he was elected, I imagine most folks did not feel that their lives were significantly changed for the better.

Pursuing the things this world values—political power and wealth is guaranteed to bring emptiness. This is Satan’s pattern—he always over-promises and under-delivers.

This was what he did when he tempted Jesus, “All these things will I give thee, if thou wilt fall down and worship me” (Matthew 4:8). All of the things Satan offered, nothing compared with the glory that Jesus eventually received from the road that led to the cross.

In the same way, Satan would like to distract Christians from seeking the things that are valuable, and that will bring hope. Satan tells Christians that politics will not only change the world for the better, it is an easier way to change the world.

The Bible is clear that we build hope as we nurture our relationship with God and then work to help our brothers and sisters build that same relationship in their own lives. The reason that we can hope is not because people are so wonderful—we don’t have to live very long to realize that they aren’t. The reason we hope is because we serve an awesome, faithful God who walks with us through the worst of our trials.

Remember that We Have Undeserved Hope

Jesus’ messages about forgiveness make it clear that one of the major reasons that we have for forgiving others in our lives is that we have received great and undeserved forgiveness. The same is true for hope.

Each one of us was hopeless and without reason to expect to receive hope and we were still given a ray of light in the midst of our darkness. Maybe part of the reason that we have so much trouble hoping for good things for the people around us is that we do not remember how hopeless we were before we found grace.

If Jesus was able to bring hope to our hopeless existence, then certainly He can do wonderful things in the hearts and lives of others around us. The only people we should give up on are the ones that our Savior has given up on as well.

Small Efforts Do Make a Difference

I remember having a conversation with a young person who was planning to go into medicine and had a plan to go to a foreign country and serve the people there. As we were talking, an older man entered the conversation and shared that he saw little hope for change in developing countries.

The people in those countries just weren’t interested in getting better and didn’t do the minimum necessary to stave off things like worms and parasites. Doctors and nurses couldn’t make a difference in such an environment.

I could sense the heart of the youth sinking as this older man shared. He had experience, and he had given up hope. The sad thing was that he was also stealing the hope of someone who still had a desire to serve.

When I was in training, I had a surgeon tell me that family doctors didn’t really do anything. They simply kept their patients alive till their next office visit, whereas surgeons really “fixed” people—taking out (or off) the offending body part.

At the end of the day, small efforts do make a difference. I don’t do brain surgery, but I still can make a difference in someone else’s life— maybe just by spending a little time and listening and praying. This is true for all of us.

More than that, we come to realize that making this effort changes our own lives for the better. Jesus told the sheep that as they ministered to “the least of these my brethren,” they were ministering to Him.

Even if no one’s life is improved, our Savior knows our desires and feels our efforts, and will reward them someday.

A Few Things to Remember

When we face failures, we tend to move in one of two directions. Those of us who are optimists tend to believe that this episode was an isolated event and that the future is still bright. On the other hand, pessimists believe that failures are permanent, personal, and pervasive.

Pessimists believe that their failures are the result of intrinsic character flaws that they have and that these things affect all of their lives and are unlikely to change. Unlike the righteous man who falls to rise again, these people fall and lie where they fall, defeated at the outset.

When we are dealing with other people, we need to give them the same grace that we should give ourselves. They, too, are growing, and if they have a failure today, they will do better tomorrow. Maybe they will fail again, but they will at least “fail better.”

Conclusion

Cynicism is rife in our world. Many have given up hope for a better future, and it is understandable for those who have invested their hope in this world’s institutions. There is no real hope in government or in armies or in bureaucracy.

The song says, “Oh to have no hope in Jesus, how dark this world must be!” For, Jesus is the one who brings light into our darkness and allows us to continue, even when others fail us.

God is the one who redeems us. He is the one who sent the prophets, even though their messages were ignored, and the prophets were persecuted. He is the one who continues to hope for us, even when we have failed Him so many times in the past.

He is the reason we carry on. He is the reason that we have hope, not only for ourselves but also for our brothers.

“Dk. Waldron, Elsie anahitaji msaada!” Mume wa Elsie alikuwa msimamo, karibu hasira, alipoitazama. Kwa upande mmoja, Elsie alikuwa akiitazama sakafu, karibu kama kuwa hayupo kabisa. Sikuwahi kukutana na wawili hao kabla na nilikuwa nikiwahi kidogo kuelewa ni nini kinahitajika kwangu ili kumsaidia.

“Nini kinaendelea?” niliuliza nikipitia rekodi yake. Hiyo ilikuwa bado nyakati za rekodi za karatasi, na nikaelekea sehemu ya maabara ya rekodi yake. Hakukuwa na chochote kigumu sana nilichoona huko—enzayimu za ini zake zilikuwa zikipanda kidogo, lakini vinginevyo, kila kitu kilionekana sawa.

“Ni tabia yake ya kunywa!” Mume wake aliniambia. “Anakunywa zaidi na zaidi kila jioni. Haatoki isipokuwa kununua wiski. Anakunywa hadi atoroke fahamu kila usiku na lazima apewe kitu kila asubuhi ili kuanza siku yake.”

“Je, hilo ni kweli?” niliuliza Elsie, nikiwa nimejisikia kama jaji anayeangalia kesi ya juri.

“Ndiyo,” alijibu. Uso wake haukuonyesha hisia yoyote, na sikuweza kusema je, alikuwa anataka kuhudhuria au la.

“Unataka msaada?” niliimuuliza. Hili lilikuwa swali lenye mzigo. Watu wengi wanaotatizika na uraibu wa pombe hawako tayari kutoroka mtego wake mgumu. Labda Elsie alikuwa tofauti.

“Nadhani ndiyo,” alisema bila kujali. Mara nyingine tena, sikuweza kujua kama alitaka kuwa pale au la.

“Kwa kiwango unachokunywa, utaua nafsi yako ndani ya mwaka mmoja—labda miwili kwa heri—ikiwa hautaacha kabisa pombe,” nilimwambia. “Ikiwa unataka, nitajaribu kukuokoa nafasi ya ndani ya hospitali kwa ajili ya kutolewa sumu ya pombe na kukusaidia kuacha pombe.”

“Yeye yuko tayari,” mume wake alisema kwa hakika.

Unaposhughulika na mtu anayekunywa kwa wingi, ni muhimu kwamba wasiache kunywa ghafla bila msaada wa matibabu. Kuacha pombe ghafla husababisha mwili kuingia katika kutokwa na dalili za kujiondoa ambazo zinaweza kutoa hali inayoitwa Delirium Tremens na hata kuleta mshtuko wa mwili.

Nilitoka chumba cha uchunguzi kwenda kupiga simu. Si rahisi kamwe kupata mahali pa kumwwekea mtu ajaribu kurekebishwa kutoka kwa aina yoyote ya kemikali, na ilichukua zaidi ya saa moja na nusu kabla sikuona kituo kilichokuwa tayari kumchukua Elsie na kumsaidia kuacha wiski.

Nikongojea niliporudi chumbani kwake. Nilikuwa nikiona kuwa nisingeweza kupata mahali pa kumpeleka.

Niliwaambia kuhusu mpango, na mume wake alikubali kwa kusugua kichwa kwa nguvu, wakati Elsie aliendelea kutazama sakafu kimya. “Tunaweza kuomba pamoja kabla ya kuondoka?” niliwauliza, na walipokubali, niliwaombea pamoja nao, nikiomba uhuru na uwepo wa Yesu katika maisha yao yote mawili.

Waliacha ofisi yangu na maagizo ya kwenda na maelekezo ya mahali pa kwenda. Nilihisi furaha kwa mchana mzima, nikijua kuwa nilifanya jitihada za ziada na kweli nilifanya tofauti katika maisha ya jamaa wa umri wa kati.

Katikati ya saa nane mchana, nilipokea simu kutoka kituo cha kurekebisha tabia. Hawakuonekana hata kivuli cha Elsie wala mumewe, jambo lililoniibua kushangaa, kwa kuwa siku ilikuwa ya jua na kituo hicho hakikuwa mbali sana. Kwa kuhisi uzito moyoni, nikapiga nambari ya jamaa hao.

“Hajaendi!” mume wake alinieleza. “Ananiambia alinikuambia hii mapema. Atajaribu kupunguza, lakini hapendi kuingia kituoni au kitu chochote kama hicho. Nadhani mwambie tu tutaowajulisha ikiwa atabadilisha mawazo.”

Nurse wangu alipigia simu kituo hicho na kuwaambia habari mbaya, na nikakaa kitandani changu, nikishtuka. Ningeweza kufanya nini zaidi? Je, kulikuwa na suluhisho kwa Elsie—msemo tofauti ningeweza kusema ungelifanya mabadiliko katika maisha yake?

Kuhusu mwaka baadaye, nilipokea habari mbaya kwamba Elsie alikuwa amefariki nyumbani. Nilihakika mambo yangekuwa tofauti kama angeenda rehabi na kama angeweka udhibiti kwa Yesu. Hakukuwa na lolote kati ya hilo, na nilihisi ucheshi ukibanuka moyoni mwangu.

Ucheshi

Tunaishi katika enzi ya ucheshi. Katika Ugiriki ya kale, wacheshi walikuwa kundi la wanaume waliotofautiana ambao walijulikana kwa kuwa wagumu wa tabia na kusema maneno mabaya (wangeweza kusema ya kweli) kwa watu. Mara nyingi walivaa taya na walitenda kwa namna ambayo Waatheni wengi walifurahia kuto kuwa karibu nao.

Leo, ucheshi unamaanisha mwelekeo wa kuamini mabaya kuhusu watu na hali. Watu wa kienyeji wanaamini kuwa watu wote wanachochewa kwa tamaa za kibinafsi pekee na kwamba matukio mabaya yatatawala.

Daktari wengi vijana wana matarajio mema na matumaini makubwa. Wanaamini kwamba wakichukua juhudi kubwa kabisa, wanaweza kufanya athari nzuri na halisi katika maisha ya wagonjwa wao. Kwa bahati mbaya, kadri muda unavyopita na wanapojaribu kwa uwezo wao wote na wagonjwa hawabadiliki, wanaweza kukata tamaa. Waganga hawa bado wanajaribu, lakini hawatahitaji tena kwa dhati kwamba juhudi zao zitaleta tofauti kubwa.

Inaonekana kwamba watu wanaohusishwa na siasa mara nyingi wana nia njema. Wanaziiona hii kama njia ya kubadilisha jamii kwa heri. Kwa bahati mbaya, kadri muda unavyopita na uso wa viongozi unavyobadilika, sera hazibadiliki sana, wanakosa matumaini.

Wakati mwingine ucheshi huu umeelekezwa dhidi ya wanasiasa wote. Wakati mwingine ni ghadhabu tu iliyolengwa dhidi ya wanachama wa chama kinachopingana na mrengo wao. Matumaini yanachukuliwa na ucheshi.

Ucheshi katika Biblia

Ikiwa kuna kitabu katika Biblia kinachoonekana kama kimeandikwa na mtu mcheshi, ni kitabu cha Mhubiri. Mhubiri, ambaye tunaelewa kuwa ni Sulemani, anataja mambo yote aliyoyajaribu katika jaribio la kutafuta furaha.

Katika sura ya 2:17-23 Sulemani anabainisha kazi kama ya bure. Anakamilisha kwa kusema, “Kwa maana yeye hajapata kibichi cha kazi zake zote, wala kwa msongo wa moyo wake, kwa kazi yake aliyofanya chini ya jua? Kwa sababu siku zake zote ni maumivu, na mambo yake yote ni huzuni; moyo wake haitulii usiku. Hii pia ni ubatili.” (Mhubiri 2:22,23)

Aliona dunia ikiendeshwa na watawala wa ukandamizaji na wazee waliona hawana yanaweza kufanya mengi. Sulemani alifika mbali hata kusema kwamba mamlaka ya kisiasa haikuwa na maana: “Bora mtoto maskini mwenye busara kuliko mfalme mzee mwenye upumbavu, ambaye hasi kuonyeshwa: kwa sababu kutoka gerezani huingia kwa enzi; naye aliyezaliwa katika ufalme wake hunyolewa.” (Mhubiri 4:13)

Katika Mhubiri 6:6, anaonekana kudharau maisha marefu. “Kweli, hata kama angeishi miaka elfu mara mbili, bado hakufanya wema: hapana wote wanakwenda mahali pamoja?”

Bila shaka, anakamilisha kitabu chake kifupi kwa maagizo ya kumkumbuka Muumba wetu katika siku za ujana. Kuna baraka kwa wale wanaochagua kumkazia Mungu wanapokuwa bado na nishati kidogo badala ya wakapozeeka na kukatishwa tamaa, kama Sulemani.

Baadaye, ilionekana karibu kama Mungu alikuwa amekata tamaa kwa watu wake. Hata hivyo aliendelea kutuma manabii kwao, lakini alijua bila shaka kwamba watu wangekataa kuwasiliana. “Kwa hiyo utasema maneno yote haya kwao; lakini hawatasikiliza: utakiliita nao; lakini hawatajibu.” (Yeremia 7:27)

Hata katika Agano Jipya, Paulo alimwambia Timotheo kwamba wakati utakuja watu wasiosikiliza mafundisho yenye afya. “Kwa kuwa kutakuwepo wakati wasiotii mafundisho yenye afya; lakini kwa tamaa zao wenyewe watajikusanya walimu, wenye masikio ya kutojuta;” (2 Timotheo 4:3).

Kwa kuchagua na kupendelea aya hizi, tunaweza kutoka na mtazamo wa giza juu ya siku za usoni na, haswa, juu ya hiari ya binadamu ya kubadilika. Inaonekana hakuna maana ya kuwekeza nafsi zetu kwa watu waliotuzunguka. Wamejaa taabu na wanaonekana kubadilika kama chipmunk atakavyoweza kumudu hesabu za utofauti.

Mpinzani wa Ucheshi

Mpinzani wa ucheshi ni matumaini. Ni imani kwamba maisha ya baadaye yanaweza kuwa bora.

Ni ya kushangaza kwamba Mtume Paulo alizungumza kuhusu taabu katika Waraka kwa Waroma, “Na si hayo peke yake; bali tunajivunia katika taabu pia; tukijua kwamba taabu huleta uvumilivu; na uvumilivu, majaribio; na majaribio, matumaini; na matumaini hayaudanganyi; kwa sababu upendo wa Mungu umefurushwa moyoni mwetu kwa Roho Mtakatifu aliyezotolewa kwetu.” (Waroma 5:3-5).

Huenda hatujafikia mahali tunajivunia majaribu tunayopitia, lakini bila shaka, yanatupatia vitu vingine anavyozitaja. Kwa sababu, tunaongezeka katika uvumilivu na uzoefu, hata tunapokabiliana na majaribu, lakini zaidi ya hayo, tunaona kuwa tuna matumaini ya kesho kwa sababu tutumikia Mungu Mkuu.

Tofauti katika hadithi ya Mwanamume Aliyetoweka wa Luka 15 inatufundisha mengi kuhusu matumaini. Baba na kaka mkubwa walikuwa tofauti kabisa kwa mtazamo wao.

Baba hakuwahi kukata tamaa—alijua kwamba mwanawe alikuwa amemkosea na kuenda mbali na yale aliyoyajua kuwa ni mema, lakini bado baba alitaka kuona mtumwa akirudi na kugeuka.

Kinyume chake, kaka mkubwa hakuwa na matumaini kwa kaka yake mdogo; alikuwa pia mwenye hasira kwake. Mwana aliyepotea alikuwa ametumia pesa zake kwa ovyo, alikuwa ameishi katika dhambi, na sasa, alirudi nyumbani kwa sababu hakukuwa na pesa.

Bila shaka, hakukuwa na sababu ya kumwamini mwana mdogo. Hata hivyo, hivyo ndicho Baba yetu wa Mbinguni anachotufanyia sisi.

Tafuta Matumaini Katika Maeneo Sahihi

Sehemu ya tatizo ni kwamba tunatafuta matumaini katika maeneo yasiyo sahihi. Miaka kadhaa iliyopita, mgombea urais aliwania nafasi kwa kauli mbiu “Matumaini na Mabadiliko,” na ingawa alichaguliwa, nawaza wengi hawakuhisi maisha yao yamebadilika kwa kiasi kikubwa kuwa bora.

Kufuata vitu vinavyothaminiwa na dunia—nguvu za kisiasa na utajiri vinahakikisha kuleta upungufu wa maana. Hii ni mbinu ya Shetani—daima anatoa ahadi kubwa na hatimaye hatoleta matokeo.

Hili ndilo alilofanya alipomjaribu Yesu, “Vitu vyote hivi nitakupa, ikiwa utakunyenyekeza ukaniabudu mimi” (Mathayo 4:8). Vitu vyote ambavyo Shetani alitoa, hayakuwa na kulinganishwa na utukufu ambao Yesu hatimaye alipokea kupitia njia iliyompelekea msalabani.

Kwa njia ile ile, Shetani angependa kumvutia Mkristo asitafute vitu vyenye thamani, ambavyo vitaleta matumaini. Shetani huwaambia Wakristo kwamba siasa hazitabadilisha tu dunia kwa heri, bali ni njia rahisi zaidi ya kuibadilisha dunia.

Biblia ni wazi kuwa tunajenga matumaini tunapokuza uhusiano wetu na Mungu kisha tukasaidia ndugu zetu kujenga uhusiano huo katika maisha yao. Sababu tunayo matumaini si kwa sababu watu ni wazuri sana—hatuhitaji kuishi kwa muda mrefu sana kuona kuwa si. Sababu tunatumaini ni kwa sababu tunamtumikia Mungu wa ajabu, mwaminifu anayepitia nasi kupitia majaribu mabaya zaidi.

Kumbuka Kwamba Tuna Matumaini Yasiyotokana na Tunayo Stahili

Ujumbe wa Yesu kuhusu msamaha unaonyesha wazi kuwa moja ya sababu kuu tunazopaswa kumsamehe mwingine ni kwa sababu tumepokea msamaha mkubwa na usiotukutarajia. Hali hiyo inahusiana pia na matumaini.

Kila mmoja wetu alikuwa bila matumaini na bila sababu ya kutegemea kupata matumaini, na bado tulipokezwa na miale ya mwanga katikati ya giza letu. Labda sehemu ya sababu tunapata shida ya kutumaini mema kwa watu waliotuzunguka ni kwa sababu hatukumbuki jinsi tulivyokuwa bila matumaini kabla hatujapata neema.

Ikiwa Yesu aliweza kuleta matumaini katika maisha yetu yasiyo na matumaini, basi bila shaka Yeye anaweza kufanya mambo makubwa katika mioyo na maisha ya wengine waliotuzunguka. Watu pekee tunayopaswa kuwaameza ni wale ambao Mwokozi wetu pia amewaachia.

Jitihada Ndogo Zinafanya Tofauti

Ninakumbuka mazungumzo niliyokuwa nayo na kijana aliyepanga kujiingiza katika tiba na alikuwa na mpango wa kwenda nchi za kigeni kuhudumia watu huko. Tulipokuwa tukiongea, mzee mmoja alijiingiza mazungumzo na kusema kuwa hakuona matumaini mengi ya mabadiliko katika nchi zinazoendelea.

Watu katika nchi hizo hawakuwa na hamu ya kuboresha hali yao na hawakufanya kiwango cha chini kinachohitajika kuzuia vitu kama minyoo na viumbe wanaoishi ndani ya miili. Madaktari na wauguzi hawawezi kuleta tofauti katika mazingira kama hayo.

Niliweza kuhisi moyo wa kijana huyo ukishuka alipozungumziwa na mzee huyo. Alikuwa na uzoefu, na alikuwa amekata tamaa. Jambo la kusikitisha ni kwamba alikuwa pia anawatoza tumaini mtu aliyekuwa bado na hamu ya kuhudumu.

Nilikua nikipata mafunzo, daktari mmoja aliyekuwa fundi wa upasuaji aliniambia kuwa madaktari wa familia hawafanyi chochote kwa kweli. Wanamuweka mgonjwa hai hadi ziara yao inayofuata, wakati upasuaji unarekebisha watu—kutokwa au kuondolewa kwa sehemu ya mwili inayosababisha tatizo.

MWishowe, jitihada ndogo hufanya tofauti. Sijafanya upasuaji wa ubongo, lakini bado ninaweza kufanya tofauti katika maisha ya mtu—labda kwa kutumia muda kidogo kusikiliza na kuomba. Hii ni kweli kwa kila mmoja wetu.

Zaidi ya hayo, tunagundua kwamba kufanya jitihada hizi kunabadilisha maisha yetu wenyewe kwa heri. Yesu aliwaambia kondoo kwamba walipomhudumia “wa wadogo wa ndugu zangu hawa,” walikuwa wamhudumia Yeye.

Hata kama maisha ya mtu hayabadilishi, Mwokozi wetu anajua matamanio yetu, anahisi jitihada zetu, na atazifidia siku moja.

Mambo Machache ya Kukumbuka

Tunapokumbana na kushindwa, tunaelekea katika moja ya mwelekeo miwili. Wale wetu ambao ni wana matumaini wanakisia kuwa tukio hili lilikuwa la kujitokeza pekee na kwamba siku za usoni bado ni angavu. Kwa upande mwingine, walio na malumbano wanaamini kuwa kushindwa ni kudumu, binafsi, na kunaathiri kila kitu.

Wanao dharau wanaamini kuwa kushindwa kwao ni matokeo ya dosari za tabia walizonazo na kwamba mambo haya yanaathiri maisha yao yote na hayatarahisiki kubadilika. Tofauti na mtu mwenye haki ambaye anashuka ili kuinuka tena, watu hawa wanaanguka na kukaa pale walipopaa, wakiwa wamefukuzwa tangu mwanzo.

Wakati tunashughulika na watu wengine, tunahitaji kuwapa neema ile ile tunayopaswa kuipatia sisi wenyewe. Hao pia wanakua, na ikiwa wana kushindwa leo, watafanya vizuri kesho. Labda watashindwa tena, lakini angalau watashindwa kwa njia nzuri zaidi.”

Hitimisho

Ucheshi umeenea katika dunia yetu. Wengi wameshatoa tamaa kwa ajili ya siku zijazo bora, na ni rahisi kueleweka kwa wale waliowekeza matumaini yao katika taasisi za dunia. Hakuna matumaini ya kweli katika serikali au jeshi au katika utumishi wa umma.

Wimbo unasema, “Ee kutokuwepo kwa matumaini kwa Yesu, dunia ingekuwa jeusi kiasi gani!” Kwa maana Yesu ndiye anayetoa nuru katika giza letu na kuturuhusu kuendelea, hata wakati wengine wanatikisa matumaini yetu.

Mungu ndiye anayeturejesha. Yeye ndiye aliyetuma manabii, ingawa ujumbe wao ulipuuzwa, na manabii wakasumbuliwa. Yeye ndiye anayeeendelea kutumaini kwetu, hata tukiwa tumekosea kwa nyakati nyingi za zamani.

Yeye ndiye sababu tunavyoendelea. Yeye ndiye sababu tunayo matumaini, si tu kwa ajili yetu wenyewe bali pia kwa ajili ya ndugu zetu.
